title: AI can uncover humanity's unknown unknowns
subtitle: How machines can teach us to think differently
author: Jessie Hall
introduction: The AI system AlphaGo discovered strategies in the game of Go that human beings didn't even know that they didn't know. AI then is capable of discovering both known unknowns and unknown unknowns in fields from games to protein folding. Hall and Vold here argue we should therefore not only see AI as a tool, but as a teacher. We should learn new ways to think from AI, not only focus on its outcomes. We should learn how the AI beat us at Go, rather than just lamenting our defeat.
body:
This is part 2 of a 2-part series on AI and Human Creativity. Read Part 1 on the dangers of AI to human creativity by Armin Schulz.

Contemporary Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can not only outperform humans in certain tasks, but they are also able to do things that humans have not yet figured out — such as identifying entirely new strategies to beat World Champions at the strategy game Go. As intellectual work that was once uniquely human is increasingly performed by machines, popular literature on the present and future of AI tends to focus on ethical concerns of bias and fairness, misinformation and fraud, human replacement, and alienation. While there is plenty to worry about, there are also reasons for optimism. AI is moving from simply being faster and more powerful at processing information in otherwise human-discovered domains of knowledge to actively expanding those domains. We now need to try to understand and learn from our machine counterparts because they are our best bet for solving pressing real-world problems.

SUGGESTED VIEWING AI is a mirror on humanity With Shannon Vallor

The idea of learning from machines is not new. Several early 20th century developmental psychologists, most notably Jean Piaget and Lev Vygotsky, were keenly interested in methods of learning with external aids. Discussions in contemporary philosophy of cognitive science have used these ideas to support ‘situated views’ of cognition — views that emphasize the extent to which the human mind is embodied, embedded, and extended into the world beyond the biological brain. During the height of the Cold War, there were notable efforts to develop ‘teaching machines’ in both the US and the USSR. Prominent thinkers like psychologist B.F. Skinner promoted the idea that machines could efficiently train masses of students. These ideas were intertwined with the birth of cybernetics, a field whose emphasis on feedback and automated control in human and computer systems was attractive to many Cold War technologists. But none of this work explicitly develops a view of how we could use contemporary machine learning systems as external devices to scaffold human learning.

One very basic and yet key observation of human learning is that we often learn from one another. At school, teachers help us to acquire skills like reading and mathematical reasoning. Vygotsky conceptualized this learning process as taking place between a more knowledgeable other (MKO) and a child learner. The MKO provides scaffolding for the child learner, lending support where the child cannot yet accomplish a task on their own. In Vygotsky’s model, the MKO gradually reduces guidance and support as the child acquires greater understanding of the target task. Vygotsky identifies this phase of skill acquisition as the zone of proximal development (ZPD), which is perhaps his most famous contribution to developmental psychology. In this ZPD, a child still needs support — or scaffolding — for a particular task, but gradually requires less and less support, until the child has mastered the task enough to perform it independently.

In typical human cognitive skill development under this model, there is a ‘soft constraint’ on what can be learned: whatever it is that an MKO can demonstrate. A task for which there is no MKO (or a task for which there is limited knowledge in general) is, in a pragmatic sense, a task that cannot be taught. This constraint is ‘soft’ in the sense that it is far from an absolute limit on what can be learned*.* Cognitive scientists often talk about creativity as the capacity of cognitive agents to extend and transfer learned skills to new domains and novel problems. Humans learn things that are not explicitly taught all the time — from conjuring new theorems and proofs using a suite of basic axioms, to theorizing about quantum mechanics by upending long-held metaphysical assumptions like causal determinism.

At the same time, there are things we do not, and even cannot know, given our cognitive limitations. An individual human, for instance, cannot run through every possible board arrangement for the game of Go to inform their next move. In fact, this is not something even very powerful computers can do. The number of possible legal board positions in the game of Go is on the order of magnitude of 10170, which is profoundly more than the estimated number of atoms in the observable universe. To play Go, humans learn the rules of Go. But to play Go well, humans rely on heuristics — rules of thumb or play ‘wisdom’ – guidelines that are meant to steer toward winning strategy. These heuristics (often captured in short proverbs (e.g., capture the cutting stones) are acquired through experience, and passed from MKOs to learners. Human learning of Go, then, is a combination of creativity (inventing heuristics and strategies from experience and game knowledge) and demonstrative learning (a new player being told by an MKO ‘when in doubt, tenuki’).

AI systems can find and analyse patterns across more variables than humans can mentally track, and the patterns they identify don’t always map onto the intuitions that shape the patterns that humans are likely to notice and understand. When Google DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat the International Champion Go player Lee Sedol in 2016, it did so without the heuristics that guide human play — no explicit representation of the Go-playing wisdom that guided human players was programmed into AlphaGo. However, AlphaGo was initially trained on Go games played between a range of amateur players, and it may have implicitly learned heuristics that guided these players. But AlphaGo subsequently trained by playing against different versions of itself, discovering its own strategies — strategies unknown even to the developers of the program. AlphaGo is credited with inventing completely new joseki (reliable sequences of moves, much like book moves in chess). As a result of its innovations, AlphaGo does not always abide by conventional wisdom. This is most famously illustrated by AlphaGo’s move 37 in game 2 of the match with Lee Sedol, a move which impressed fellow professional players with its creativity, brilliance, and element of surprise. Because of its innovations, AlphaGo has had an impact on the way human players approach and think about Go — it has become an MKO.

To gain understanding and appreciation for AlphaGo’s moves, it helps to know why AlphaGo made the moves it did. The developers of AlphaGo were able to examine AlphaGo’s decision-making process for any given move — they noted for instance that AlphaGo had judged the odds of a human making move 37 to be around 1/10,000, but it also judged that the move would positively influence the odds of winning. In place of the concepts and heuristics that human players use, AlphaGo used a more probabilistic framework to detect relationships that lay outside of human intuitions.

For players without the privilege of developer access to AlphaGo’s decision process, DeepMind has released a program called AlphaGo Teach, which allows players to see AlphaGo’s evaluation of winning odds move by move, for any move a player selects, as well as the odds that a human player would make the selected move. AlphaGo Teach thus allows players to understand novel approaches and to come to a deeper understanding of the conventional wisdom that has guided play in the past.

Two things bear emphasizing. First, one could argue that AlphaGo genuinely expanded the possibilities of Go because previously unheard-of playing strategies emerged as a result of AlphaGo’s win-maximizing approach, strategies which human Go players are rapidly integrating into their own play. But, perhaps even more significantly, AlphaGo has facilitated a new means of approaching the task space — not just the strategies themselves but what informs them — and how to reason through and justify moves. Gaining insight into how particular moves relate to winning odds, for instance, has helped players better understand the game of Go in general, and seeing the odds of human choices gives great insight into Go as it is actually played. One could envision novel research programs developed from such insight: parsing the strategic wisdom derived from human psychology from the rule-based wisdom derived from formal constraints of the game.

AI could offer alternative frameworks for processing and synthesizing information, frameworks that diverge from human patterns of reasoning and cognitive biases, and it could do so in higher-stakes domains.

AlphaGo has essentially provided additional insight into a sea of ‘unknown unknowns’. In the unfathomable possibility space of moves in Go, it is impossible to know how every game could unfold — a known unknown. The limits of learned strategy are an unknown unknown; we do not know what strategies we do not know. AlphaGo has also demonstrated some previously unknown limits to conventional wisdom by clarifying some previously illegible caveats to the norms of play. From the perspective of thinking about AlphaGo as a potential teacher — as an MKO — this is truly exciting. Better game play is not the only domain in which AI technology could guide, enhance, or accelerate human capabilities. AI could offer alternative frameworks for processing and synthesizing information, frameworks that diverge from human patterns of reasoning and cognitive biases, and it could do so in higher-stakes domains.

Beyond matters of strategy, AI has advanced work on another problem of vexing computational complexity: protein folding. Understanding how proteins fold is critical to work on everything from the evolution of organisms to the etiologies and mechanisms of diseases. Until recently, this work was incredibly time-consuming, complex, and difficult because the geometry of a protein is determined by an uncontrollable number of variables, from the amino acids involved, to the physical variables influencing each atom, to the temperature, pressure, and acidity of the environment, and that’s leaving aside things like mutations and misfoldings. In 2020, Google DeepMind released a program, AlphaFold2, that could model proteins based on amino acid profiles, while also providing a confidence score for the configuration predicted. While humans had tried to map the step-by-step physical process of protein folding, Alphafold2 learned to predict final protein structures directly from patterns in sequence data, skipping those intermediate steps. The outcome of this was widely regarded as a milestone that could revolutionize structural biology. In 2024, AlphaFold2’s creators were awarded a Nobel Prize for their achievements. Shortly thereafter, researchers at Harvard developed an open-source version of AlphaFold2 called OpenFold. Earlier this year, DeepMind released its latest iteration, AlphaFold3. Thanks to these advances, biologists now have access to over 200 million protein models — orders of magnitude more than had been painstakingly modelled by earlier methods since the 1960s.

Can the patterns detected by AlphaFold3 or OpenFold facilitate further understanding of the underlying mechanisms of protein folding, in the way that AlphaGo has informed gameplay in Go? Deep learning models, like AlphaFold3 and OpenFold, process information using high-dimensional, non-intuitive pattern recognition and can detect correlations and structures in data that humans may overlook, revealing novel inferential paths.

If we are going to think of technologies like this as a more knowledgeable other, we need to figure out how to learn from them. The key is to move beyond simply using the outputs of these technologies. We need to peer beyond their immediate behaviour, searching for the potential for new strategies, methods and modes of reasoning that they could offer us. If we’re open to it, these alternative inferential styles could inspire new heuristics or reasoning strategies in humans. More concretely, they could inspire new strategies and methodologies in domains like science and mathematics — strategies that extend beyond our natural cognitive tendencies. AI systems aren’t just solving problems faster – they are showing us new ways to think about them.
